findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Enumerate the ready_tickets backend refactor: state that ready_states (src/rebar/_engine_support/reads.py:520) currently lacks any include_body/full/lean plumbing and specify how it will invoke the shared projection function and honor full=True.
evidence: src/rebar/_engine_support/reads.py:520-524 `ready_states(...)` builds `[public_state(s) for s in find_ready_tickets(...)]` — no TicketQuery, no include_body, no full parameter

src/rebar/_snapshot/ticket_view.py:383-385 and src/rebar/_engine_support/reads.py:440 show the lean pop lives in the `list_states`/`list_by_query` path keyed on `query.include_body`, a path ready_tickets never touches

Plan text acknowledges '`ready_tickets` has **no lean mode and no limit at all**' but the AC asserts a single shared function 'restoring the previous bytes exactly' without naming the ready_states refactor required
findings.finding: The AC requires the lean projection to run 'through one function shared by both read backends', but list_tickets and ready_tickets do not currently share a projection function: list_tickets -> list_by_query -> list_states applies include_body (dropping description/comments), while ready_tickets -> rebar.ready -> ready_states -> public_state has no include_body/full/lean plumbing at all. The plan does not enumerate that ready_states (reads.py:520) must gain new lean/full plumbing to satisfy this AC.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria, bullet 'The lean projection drops authorship_ledger, attestations, signature and keyring ... through one function shared by both read backends'
scenarios: Implementer wires the drop into list_states only and ready_tickets stays unbounded/unprojected
full=True regression parity is defined against list_tickets but ready_tickets has no full parameter to restore prior bytes

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the seam that measures the budget on the exact bytes the client receives (post-js_safe_result) while still allowing a structured `response_too_large` error to be raised — e.g. move the size check into the js_safe/error-guard layer, or state that the body-level check accounts for the js_safe integer-quoting delta.
evidence: _mcp_errors.py:216-236 — install_js_safe_guard wraps the tool body: `return js_safe_result(fn(*fn_args, **fn_kwargs))`, so js_safe_result runs AFTER the body returns
_mcp_errors.py:198 — js_safe_result quotes JS-unsafe integers (rebar's 19-digit nanosecond timestamps), changing the serialized byte count vs the pre-transform value
_mcp_errors.py:100-126 — the structured-error guard also wraps the body; a raised McpEnvelopeError/RebarError must originate inside the body, before js_safe_result has run
Plan Summary confirms the discriminator is byte size (94.5 MB), so a few-bytes-per-row js_safe delta on 2,855+ rows is directionally material to a budget check
findings.finding: The AC mandates measuring the payload 'post-model_validate, post-js_safe_result' and raising a structured error on excess, but js_safe_result is applied in the guard wrapper AFTER the tool body returns (and mutates byte size by quoting 19-digit ints), while a structured RebarError can only be raised from inside the body (before js_safe_result runs). The plan does not name a seam where both transforms have completed yet a structured error is still deliverable, leaving the measurement point and the error-raising point in tension.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria, bullet 2 ('bounded at ... measured on the payload the client actually receives (post-model_validate, post-js_safe_result)')
scenarios: Budget check implemented inside list_tickets body measures the pre-js_safe_result bytes and under-counts the payload the client actually receives, admitting a payload that then exceeds budget on the wire
A store sits just under 90,000 bytes pre-quoting but over it post-quoting, so the guard passes but the client still sees an oversized response

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Extend the emitted enum's value vocabulary: add `response_too_large` to `rebar.KNOWN_ERROR_CODES` (and wire it through `error_code_for` / the MCP envelope path and docs that enumerate the vocabulary), so the AC3 structured error is a defined member rather than an undefined code.
evidence: AC3: 'produces a structured error with error_code="response_too_large" naming the match count, the byte size, the budget, and the filters to narrow with.'
src/rebar/_errors.py:48-66 defines KNOWN_ERROR_CODES as a closed frozenset that does NOT include 'response_too_large'.
docs/output-schemas.md:202-203: MCP envelope `error` is 'drawn from the shared `rebar.KNOWN_ERROR_CODES` vocabulary (classified by `rebar.error_code_for`)'.

tests/interfaces/contracts/test_mcp_error_envelope_heldout.py:199-200 asserts CLI literals are a subset of KNOWN_ERROR_CODES; :218 and :267/:278 assert emitted `error` values are members — a new code absent from the vocabulary fails these held-out contract tests.
findings.finding: AC3 introduces error_code="response_too_large" for the MCP structured-error contract consumed by LLM/agent clients, but the plan never adds that value to the closed `rebar.KNOWN_ERROR_CODES` enum vocabulary (nor updates `error_code_for` / the docs that enumerate it). The value vocabulary that the emitted enum draws from is left undefined for the new code.
scenarios: An over-budget list_tickets emits error_code="response_too_large"; the held-out envelope contract test rejects it as a code absent from KNOWN_ERROR_CODES.
An MCP client branching on the documented KNOWN_ERROR_CODES vocabulary receives a code it cannot recognize because the vocabulary was never extended.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a bullet to AC3 (or the lean-projection AC) requiring `response_too_large` be added to `KNOWN_ERROR_CODES` in src/rebar/_errors.py, classified by `error_code_for`, and listed in docs/output-schemas.md, with the held-out envelope contract tests updated to accept it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Strengthen the over-budget regression assertion to check the structured error payload fields explicitly: error_code == 'response_too_large', the reported match count equals the fixture row count, and byte size, budget, and filter-hint fields are present.
evidence: Error AC: 'a structured error with error_code="response_too_large" naming the match count, the byte size, the budget, and the filters to narrow with'
Regression AC only says the over-budget store 'is refused' with no assertion on the emitted payload
E6 taxonomy item (5): missing cardinality assertion when the criterion names a count
findings.finding: The regression-coverage AC verifies the over-budget store is 'refused' but does not require asserting the CONTENTS of the structured error — the error_code=response_too_large, the match count, byte size, budget, and filter hints named in the error-contract AC. A test that only asserts a refusal (e.g. any exception) can pass while the error omits the count/size/filters the caller needs.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria — final regression bullet ('a synthetic store of >=4,000 rows (over budget) is refused')
scenarios: Refusal path returns a bare exception or an error missing the match-count/filter hints and the regression test still passes green
findings.suggested_fix: In the over-budget regression test, assert on the structured artifact (e.g. jq -e / dict access): error_code=='response_too_large', match_count == fixture_row_count (4000), byte_size present and > 90000, budget == 90000, and a non-empty filters field.

evidence: 2 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Place the byte-budget guard (and structured response_too_large decision) in the shared read seam consumed by all three ingress paths, not only at the MCP post-js_safe_result boundary, so CLI and library-facade callers of list_tickets/ready_tickets inherit the same bound.
evidence: 'measured on the payload the client actually receives (post-model_validate, post-js_safe_result)' — js_safe_result is the MCP serialization step
'one function shared by both read backends' addresses the PROJECTION but not necessarily the BYTE-BUDGET GUARD placement
rebar ingress paths: CLI in src/rebar/_commands/, MCP server, and library facades all reach the same read/reducer path
findings.finding: The response_too_large byte-budget guard is placed at the MCP-serialized payload boundary (post-js_safe_result); CLI and library-facade ingress paths that call list_tickets/ready_tickets reach the same reducer rows without passing through js_safe_result, so they inherit no bound.
findings.location: AC: 'bounded ... measured on the payload the client actually receives (post-model_validate, post-js_safe_result)'
scenarios: A library caller invoking the rebar.* list facade against this store still materializes the full unbounded row set — the bound is skippable by not going through the MCP handler.
A CLI `list`/`ready` command reaches the same read backend and emits the full payload with no response_too_large error, since js_safe_result is MCP-specific.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute the budget check on the shared read backend's canonical serialized size (used by all ingress) rather than the MCP-only js_safe_result output, or explicitly scope the AC to state the bound is intentionally MCP-only and why CLI/library callers do not need it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Justify choosing a refuse-with-`response_too_large` bound over MCP's standard cursor-based pagination (and the in-repo `_iter_cursor_pages`/ADR-0062 pattern) for `list_tickets`/`ready_tickets`, or adopt pagination; specifically address how an over-budget `ready_tickets` (which exposes no filters) can be retrieved.
evidence: Plan AC: 'Exceeding that budget produces a structured error with error_code="response_too_large" naming the match count... and the filters to narrow with. Never a partial list.'

MCP spec (retrieved modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/utilities/pagination): 'The Model Context Protocol (MCP) supports paginating list operations that may return large result sets... especially important when connecting to external services over the internet.'

In-repo prior art: cursor-based pagination via `_iter_cursor_pages` and ADR-0062 (docs/adr/0062-pagination-stall-aborts-past-fail-open.md) — the codebase already has an established pagination pattern the plan does not reference.

src/rebar/_mcp_reads.py:349 — `def ready_tickets(sort: str | None = None)`: the tool exposes NO narrowing filters, so a `response_too_large` error advising the caller to 'narrow with filters' is unactionable for ready_tickets.
ABSENCE: the plan weighs no alternative to refuse-and-narrow; pagination (spec-standard and in-repo) is never mentioned or rejected.
findings.finding: The plan sets a payload-size/scalability bound on the list operations `list_tickets` and `ready_tickets` but never considers MCP's standard cursor-based pagination — the spec's explicit remedy for list operations that return large result sets, and a pattern already implemented in this repo (`_iter_cursor_pages`, ADR-0062) — before committing to a refuse-with-`response_too_large` design. For `ready_tickets`, whose only parameter is `sort` (no filters exist), the chosen error tells the caller to 'narrow with filters' they do not have, leaving no way to retrieve a legitimately large ready set.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria (the `response_too_large` bound on list_tickets AND ready_tickets) and 'The guard that already exists' section
scenarios: A caller invokes ready_tickets on a store whose ready set exceeds 90,000 bytes: refused with response_too_large and no filter to reduce it — the tool becomes unusable, whereas pagination would return the full set in chunks.

A caller genuinely needs the whole list_tickets result over budget (e.g. a bulk export/agent scan): refuse-and-narrow forces N filtered calls the caller must stitch, versus one paginated walk the MCP client already understands.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the rollback path (and whether a flag/env toggle gates the new bound) for reverting the deployed container's list_tickets/ready_tickets behavior quickly without a code round-trip.
evidence: 'list_tickets AND ready_tickets are bounded at the same 90,000-byte ... budget'
'The lean projection drops ... recorded as a pre-1.0 breaking change'
'a fix here was previously reported complete on the strength of a merge while the deployed behaviour was still broken' — establishes a deployed runtime surface
ABSENCE: no flag/canary/staged-rollout and no rollback procedure is specified for the deployed container
findings.finding: The plan flips 100% of MCP traffic to new bounded behavior (both tools refuse over-budget payloads and lean output narrows) with no staged rollout, no feature flag, and no stated rollback path — despite operating on a deployed, long-running server the plan itself notes was previously reported fixed while still broken in production.
findings.location: Acceptance Criteria (bounding + lean-projection ACs) and 'LIVE VALIDATION' AC
scenarios: If the 90,000-byte bound is mis-calibrated in production, every list_tickets/ready_tickets call on this 2,855-ticket store starts returning response_too_large with no quick documented way to revert the deployed container to prior behavior
A client that depended on the pre-lean fields (authorship_ledger/attestations/signature/keyring) breaks at 100% cutover with no toggle to restore them without a redeploy
findings.suggested_fix: Add an AC naming how the change is reverted on the deployed server (e.g. an env var or config toggle for the budget / lean default, or a documented redeploy-of-prior-image procedure) so a mis-calibrated bound or unexpected consumer breakage can be undone without another code change.
